channel.title: Road Guide: Sonoma route
channel.description: Sonoma: I-80 → Jameson Canyon → Carneros → Sonoma → Glen Ellen → Kenwood → Santa Rosa → Sebastopol → SR 116. Play episodes in order as you drive.
channel.itunes:author: Wine Country Road Guide

item.title: 01. Welcome aboard: leaving the capital
item.description:
Good morning, Julia, Adam, and our trusty driver, and welcome aboard. I'll be your guide from the capital to the redwoods: across the floodplain, over the hills into Napa or Sonoma, and down to the Russian River at Guerneville. I'll chime in when there's something worth knowing, and keep quiet when there isn't. Tap the screen any time to see what I'm saying, or to skip me.
We're starting beside the Sacramento River, the reason this city exists at all. Sacramento grew up on the waterfront, because the river was the highway to the coast. Old Sacramento, the riverside historic district, still ha

item.title: 02. Sam Brannan, California's first millionaire
item.description: One name will follow us all day: Sam Brannan. He was a printer and a Mormon elder who sailed a shipload of Latter-day Saint emigrants round Cape Horn to California in 1846, bringing a printing press and a complete flour mill with him. He founded the California Star, San Francisco's first newspaper, and he's considered the first person to publicise the Gold Rush. His stores supplied the rush, and the profits made him California's first millionaire. He bought land everywhere, including a hot-springs valley at the far end of the Napa Valley that we may pass through later: he named it Calistoga.

item.title: 03. West Sacramento: the Town of Washington
item.description: Here's how the day's first town began: a man started a bar fight, lost it fatally, and his widow built a town. You've crossed into Yolo County and the city of West Sacramento. Its story begins with a widow. In 1849, James McDowell was shot dead in a bar argument he'd apparently started, leaving his wife Margaret with three daughters and 600 acres. She hired a surveyor, divided the land into forty-one blocks, and sold lots in a new settlement she called the Town of Washington. It became a rest stop for travellers struggling through the marshes towards Sacramento, and a busy fishing and farming

item.title: 04. The Yolo Bypass: a floodplain on purpose
item.description:
Look out at the flat land on both sides. You're on the Yolo Causeway, a three-mile viaduct across the Yolo Bypass, and this is one of the cleverest pieces of flood control in America. Rather than building ever-higher walls around Sacramento, engineers gave the river somewhere else to go.
Upstream, at a concrete spillway called the Fremont Weir, when the Sacramento River rises past a set height the excess simply pours over the top and into this basin. A second set of gates just north of West Sacramento can be opened by hand. In a big flood the bypass can carry several times the flow of the riv

item.title: 05. The causeway, the Tule Jake Road, and a quarter of a million bats
item.description:
Before any causeway, crossing this basin in the wet season meant a ferry, or a long detour south through Stockton. The first vehicle to make it across each summer set the line of the seasonal Tule Jake Road. The first causeway opened in 1916, a two-lane timber and concrete trestle, celebrated with a three-day party. In 1928 it was folded into the Lincoln Highway, the first road across America, and later carried Highway 40.
Today's twin structures date from 1962. Traffic reporters call them the long bridge and the short bridge. They're officially named for two Highway Patrol officers killed ne

item.title: 06. Davis: the university farm
item.description:
Coming up: a town so flat it calls itself the bicycling capital of America, and so practical its post office trimmed the town's own name. Coming up is Davis, a town that began as a railroad stop and became one of the most important agricultural universities on earth. The depot opened in 1868 and was named Davisville after Jerome C. Davis, a prominent local farmer. In 1907 the post office got tired of the extra syllables and shortened it to Davis.
In 1905 the state legislature passed the University Farm Bill, and Governor George Pardee chose Davis from about fifty candidate sites. Berkeley's a

item.title: 07. UC Davis and the wine revolution
item.description:
UC Davis turns up again and again in the wine story you'll hear today. In 1903 the U.S. Department of Agriculture set up an experimental vineyard at Oakville in the Napa Valley, and that Oakville Station is run by UC Davis to this day. In 1935 the heirs of the Wolfskill family, the pioneers of Winters, gave the university a hundred acres of their old ranch for an experimental orchard.
In 1951 the university produced its first graduates in viticulture and enology, the science of growing grapes and making wine. There were just seven of them, and one, Joe Heitz, went on to make one of Napa's mos

item.title: 08. The Gold Rush, and how it remade this whole region
item.description:
Let's talk about the event that made Sacramento, and in a roundabout way, much of what you'll see today.
On the 24th of January 1848, James Marshall was building a sawmill for the Sacramento pioneer John Sutter, up the American River at Coloma, when he spotted something shiny in the tailrace. It was gold. Sutter tried to keep it quiet, because he feared a rush would wreck his plans for an agricultural empire. He failed, thanks partly to Sam Brannan, who publicised it. About 300,000 people poured into California, half by sea, half overland. San Francisco went from about 200 residents in 1846 t

item.title: 09. Tule fog: the valley's winter ghost
item.description:
A practical note about this valley, especially if you ever drive it in winter. From November to March, after the first big rains, the Central Valley is prone to tule fog, named after the tule-reed wetlands that once covered it.
It's what meteorologists call radiation fog. After rain, the ground is damp and the air humid. On long, still winter nights, the ground cools quickly, and the cold air near the surface is trapped beneath warmer air above, a temperature inversion, until its moisture condenses into a thick, low blanket. It can stretch over 400 miles, from Bakersfield to Red Bluff. As of

item.title: 10. Dixon: the town that moved to the tracks
item.description:
Dixon, coming up, is a town that literally picked itself up and moved. During the Gold Rush, a settlement called Silveyville grew up here as a halfway stop for miners heading between the coast and the Sacramento gold fields. When the railroad arrived in 1868, it missed Silveyville by a few miles. So in 1871 the townspeople relocated, buildings and all, to be next to the tracks. The Methodist church on North Jefferson Street is one of the buildings from that move.
The new town was supposed to be Dicksville, after Thomas Dickson, who donated ten acres for the depot. But in 1872 the first rail s

item.title: 11. Why the valley is so flat: seven miles of buried sea floor
item.description:
This is a geology story, and it starts with a question: why is the Sacramento Valley so astonishingly flat?
The answer is that you're driving across the top of an enormous filled-in basin. During the age of the dinosaurs, between about 150 and 65 million years ago, this whole valley was a seaway. To the east, where the Sierra Nevada stands now, ran a chain of volcanoes. To the west, an ocean plate was diving beneath North America, and the rocks scraped off it piled up into a ridge that acted like a dam. Between them lay a deep basin, and the volcanoes eroded into it, shedding mud and sand dow

item.title: 12. The Patwin: the people of this valley
item.description:
Before the farms, the freeway and the university, this western edge of the Sacramento Valley was home to the Patwin, the southern branch of the Wintun peoples, who have lived in this part of California since roughly the year 500.
The Patwin lived in settled villages, fishing, hunting and gathering, and acorns were central to life: across the plains and foothills, groves of oaks were a harvest. The southern Patwin lived between what is now Suisun, Vacaville and Putah Creek, and as Spanish and later settlers pushed in, they were broken into small groups whose names survive on today's map. The U

item.title: 13. The railroad that beat the Golden Spike
item.description:
If you've noticed a railway line running alongside the freeway, it has a sneaky claim to fame.
Everyone knows the transcontinental railroad was completed with a golden spike in May 1869. What's less known is that it ended at Sacramento, short of the Pacific. Getting trains on to San Francisco Bay was a separate race.
The tracks beside you were built by the California Pacific Railroad, incorporated in 1865 to link Vallejo, on the bay, with Sacramento. Its main line from Vallejo to Washington, today's West Sacramento, was finished in November 1868, six months before the golden spike. From Janu

item.title: 14. Interstate 505: the highway that lost its letter
item.description:
Fun fact: the road you've just turned onto used to have a letter in its number. You've turned north onto Interstate 505, a quiet four-lane spur that runs about thirty miles up the western edge of the Sacramento Valley to Interstate 5. It exists so that traffic between the Bay Area and the far north of California can bypass Sacramento entirely.
It has an odd backstory. It was originally planned as part of a looping interstate called I-5W, with a W for west. The federal highway authorities later scrapped almost all of those lettered interstates, so I-5W was chopped up and renumbered: part of it

item.title: 15. The Nut Tree: a fruit stand that fed a Queen
item.description:
Near the junction with Interstate 505 is the Nut Tree, now a shopping centre, once a California legend. It opened on the 3rd of July 1921 as a little roadside fruit stand on the Lincoln Highway, run by Helen and Ed Power. It was named after a black walnut tree that grew from a nut picked up on a trail in Arizona by a pioneer girl, Sallie Fox, before she arrived in Vacaville in 1859.
By its second year the stand was serving around 950 cars a day, and it kept growing as the old highway became Interstate 80: a restaurant with a floor-to-ceiling glass aviary, a bakery, a toy shop, its own little

item.title: 16. The Delta: California's Holland
item.description:
South of the freeway, out of sight beyond the fields, lies one of the most important and most fragile landscapes in America: the Sacramento-San Joaquin River Delta. The flood water from the Yolo Bypass drains into it, and so does about half of all the water that runs off California's land, more than thirty million acre-feet a year.
Its origin is a bottleneck. Around 560,000 years ago, water broke through the coastal mountains and carved the Carquinez Strait and San Francisco Bay. All of the Central Valley's rivers had to squeeze out through that narrow gap, which slowed them down. Later, as s

item.title: 17. Vacaville and the quarrel over Rancho Los Putos
item.description: Vacaville was founded on a land deal so dodgy that one of its founders took out a newspaper notice warning people off. Vacaville is named after Juan Manuel Vaca, one of two men from New Mexico who came to California in 1841 with the Workman-Rowland Party. Vaca and his partner, Juan Felipe Peña, were granted Rancho Los Putos in 1843: over 44,000 acres, taking in all of present-day Vacaville and Lagoon Valley and stretching almost to Davis. The name comes from Putah Creek, then called the Rio de los Putos. It was General Vallejo who'd recommended the area to them. Peña's adobe home, built in 184

item.title: 18. The Vaca Mountains: the first wall of the Coast Ranges
item.description:
Here's why the other side of those hills is so much greener. The ridge rising to the west is the Vaca Mountains, the easternmost range of California's Coast Ranges, and the wall between the Sacramento Valley and everything we'll see this afternoon. Its east face rises abruptly, a thousand feet or more above the foothills. The highest point, Mount Vaca, is 2,818 feet, the top of Solano County, and the backbone is a long, level crest called the Blue Ridge.
Because they're the farthest range from the ocean, the Vacas sit in a rain shadow. They get far less rain than the Mayacamas Mountains furth

item.title: 19. From the Lincoln Highway to Interstate 80
item.description:
The road you're on has been many roads. In 1913 the Lincoln Highway was dedicated: the brainchild of an Indiana entrepreneur, Carl Fisher, and one of the first highways in America designed for cars, running from Times Square in New York to Lincoln Park in San Francisco. At first its backers declined to shift it onto the new Yolo Causeway. But in 1928, after the Carquinez Bridge opened, the Lincoln Highway was rerouted over the Yolo Causeway and through Davis, Dixon, Vacaville and Fairfield, roughly where you are now.
When the federal numbered highways arrived, this became U.S. Highway 40. Roa

item.title: 20. Jelly Belly: the President's jelly beans
item.description:
Fairfield is the home of the Jelly Belly jelly bean, and the story runs from Germany to the White House. Gustav Goelitz started a sweet business in Illinois in 1869, and the family became big in candy corn. His son Herman moved west and eventually settled the company in Oakland in 1924.
In the 1960s they started making a small, intensely flavoured mini jelly bean. Ronald Reagan, who'd given up smoking and taken to sweets instead, first tried them in 1969 and was hooked. As governor in 1973, he wrote to the company that they could hardly start a meeting without passing round the jar.
In 1976,

item.title: 21. Fairfield, Cordelia, and a captain's sense of home
item.description:
Here's a sea captain who named one town after his hometown and the next one after his wife. Fairfield and the next little place, Cordelia, were both named by one man, a clipper ship captain called Robert H. Waterman. He'd bought into Rancho Suisun, a Mexican land grant originally given in 1842 to Chief Solano, which Solano couldn't hold onto and sold to General Vallejo, who sold it on.
Waterman laid out a town in 1856 and named it after his old home of Fairfield, Connecticut. Two years later he entered it in the race to be county seat and won the title away from Benicia, helped by his offer o

item.title: 22. The Rockville Stone Chapel and a congregation split by war
item.description:
Just north of Cordelia, in the Suisun Valley, stands the Rockville Stone Chapel, built in 1856 by volunteers from local stone, cut from the nearby hills. It's a volcanic ash rock that's soft and easy to cut when quarried but hardens after it's exposed to air. The land was donated by Landy Alford, who'd come west in 1846 in the same wagon train as the ill-fated Donner Party; his son-in-law later helped rescue the survivors.
The chapel soon became a casualty of national politics. The congregation split over slavery, and at the Christmas Eve service of 1863 the northern supporters walked out. Th

item.title: 23. The Suisun Marsh
item.description:
Out to the south is a marsh where people tried for fifty years to farm, and gave up when it got too salty even for the cows. To the south lies the Suisun Marsh, described as the largest brackish-water marsh on the west coast of the United States: over a hundred thousand acres of tidal marsh, bays and sloughs, where fresh water from the Sacramento and San Joaquin rivers meets the salt of San Francisco Bay. It's named after the Suisunes, a Patwin group who lived here.
Geologically, it's made of the mountains: sediment worn off the Sierra Nevada and the Vaca Mountains, carried down by rivers and

item.title: 24. Jameson Canyon: through the hills on the Lincoln Highway
item.description:
Fun thought for this stretch: you're driving through old sea floor. You're now on Highway 12 through Jameson Canyon, the gap in the hills between Solano County and Napa. This stretch has history in its bones: in 1928 it became part of the realigned Lincoln Highway, the first road across America.
The rocks change here too. The geological maps from the Macrostrat database show the road threading past outcrops of Markley Sandstone, a white to light-grey quartz-and-mica sandstone from the Eocene, around 40 to 50 million years old. Further west come marine sandstones of the San Pablo Group from th

item.title: 25. Entering the Napa Valley
item.description:
Welcome to Napa County, and the Napa Valley. In 1981 this became the second American Viticultural Area in the country, a legally defined wine region, and it's now one of the most famous wine regions in the world, with more than 450 wineries.
Here's the layout. The valley floor rises gently north-west, from sea level here near the bay to 362 feet at Calistoga, at the foot of Mount Saint Helena. On your left as you head north will be the Mayacamas Mountains, and on your right, the Vaca Mountains we saw from the freeway. Two roads run up the valley: Highway 29 on the west side, and the quieter S

item.title: 26. Napa: a river town
item.description:
Picture Napa's Main Street in the 1850s, with up to a hundred saddle horses tied up on an ordinary afternoon. The city of Napa, off to the east, began as a river town. The Napa River is tidal here, and the town grew at its head of navigation, the furthest point boats could reach. A ship called the Susana made the first recorded trip up the river in 1842, and by 1850 the steamer Dolphin was carrying passengers.
Nathan Coombs, who'd arrived in the valley in 1845, laid out the town in 1847 and 1848 on land he'd bought from Nicolás Higuera, holder of the Mexican land grant called Rancho Entre Nap

item.title: 27. Floods, gentrification and the goddess of plenty
item.description:
For most of its history, the city of Napa was where wine-country tourists drove through, not where they stopped. That changed after a 300-million-dollar flood management project around the turn of this century widened the river and raised the bridges, and developers moved in.
The flagship was Copia, the American Center for Wine, Food and the Arts, planned and largely funded by Robert and Margrit Mondavi and named after the Roman goddess of plenty. It opened in November 2001, just two months after the September 11th attacks, with galleries, theatres, a three-and-a-half-acre kitchen garden and

item.title: 28. Who does the work? Farm labour in the valleys
item.description:
Every vineyard and orchard you pass depends on people who rarely appear in the wine brochures. The story of farm labour here is a story of successive waves.
The first workers were Native Californians, often forced: the Patwin were compelled into unpaid labour on ranches and in mines, and by 1870 the Native population of the Napa Valley consisted of only a few labourers and servants working for the settlers. In the late 1800s, Chinese and Japanese immigrants worked in Vacaville's orchards and packing houses. During the Second World War, German prisoners of war were put to work from a camp near

item.title: 29. di Rosa: moonshine, mushrooms and modern art
item.description:
Hidden off this road is the di Rosa Center for Contemporary Art, and the land has had quite a life. In 1855 it was planted with grapes and olives. In 1886 two Frenchmen built a stone winery. Then phylloxera killed the vines, and the old winery was used for growing mushrooms, making moonshine, storing grain and finally as a hay barn.
In 1960 Rene di Rosa bought it, replanted vines, and dammed an old irrigation pond, dug by Depression-era WPA workers, into a 35-acre lake. His Winery Lake vineyards eventually covered some 250 acres, and when he sold them to Seagram in 1986, he used the money to

item.title: 30. Los Carneros: the land of the rams
item.description:
These hills might look familiar: one of them may have been on your computer screen. More on that shortly. You're crossing Los Carneros, the low, rolling hills between the Napa and Sonoma valleys, along the top of San Pablo Bay. Carneros is Spanish for rams, after the sheep that once grazed these hills, and the name goes back to a Mexican land grant of 1836, Rancho Rincón de los Carneros.
This is a wine region with an unusual distinction: it was the first in California to be defined by its climate rather than by political boundaries. Being so close to the bay, it gets fog and cool breezes, so

item.title: 31. Bliss: the most famous hill in the world
item.description:
Here's a fun one, especially if you ever used a Windows XP computer. Somewhere around here, near the Napa and Sonoma county line on this very highway, is the hill in what may be the most viewed photograph in history: Bliss, the default wallpaper of Windows XP. That bright green hill under a blue sky with wispy clouds.
In January 1996, Charles O'Rear, a former National Geographic photographer who lived in St. Helena, was driving along the Sonoma Highway to visit his girlfriend. A storm had just passed, the winter rains had turned the grass a vivid green, and he noticed a hill that had been cle

item.title: 32. Schellville junction and a quarter-scale railroad
item.description:
This crossroads has two railroads: a real one that floods, and a quarter-size one that one man built himself. This crossroads is Schellville, named after Theodore Schell, who ranched nearby. It's been an important railway junction since 1888, and a two-mile-long railyard sits just south of the old depot, which is now the freight office for the SMART line. Being low beside Sonoma Creek, it floods every five to ten years in a wet winter. In March 2023, after months of rain, the waterlogged ground gave way and a train carrying corn seed derailed here, toppling four cars. Nobody was hurt.
On the

item.title: 33. The Bear Flag Revolt: a republic that lasted 25 days
item.description:
Sonoma's plaza is where California's strangest little rebellion happened.
By 1846, Mexico had largely neglected its distant province of Alta California, and Mexican officials were nervous about the growing number of Americans arriving without permission. Those immigrants, in turn, complained they weren't allowed to buy land and had been threatened with expulsion. Meanwhile, a U.S. Army explorer, Captain John C. Frémont, was camped in the Sacramento Valley, quietly encouraging trouble.
At dawn on the 14th of June 1846, a band of about thirty-three American settlers rode into Sonoma and took G

item.title: 34. The Count of Buena Vista and the birth of California wine
item.description:
Sonoma Valley calls itself the birthplace of the California wine industry, and there's a case for it. The Franciscan friars planted the valley's first vines at the mission in 1823, and Vallejo expanded them.
Then came Agoston Haraszthy, one of the great characters of the West. A Hungarian nobleman, he'd already founded a village in Wisconsin, where German settlers called him Count, and been the first town marshal and county sheriff of San Diego. In 1857, just east of Sonoma, he founded Buena Vista, one of California's first successful commercial wineries. He's often called the father of Calif

item.title: 35. Sonoma: the last mission and the largest plaza
item.description:
Welcome to Sonoma, where modern California arguably began.
When the Spanish arrived, this was near the meeting point of several Native peoples: the Coast Miwok, the Southern Pomo to the north-west, the Wappo to the north-east, and the Patwin to the east. In 1823, a Franciscan priest, José Altimira, founded Mission San Francisco Solano here. It was the twenty-first, last and northernmost of the California missions, and the only one built after Mexico won independence from Spain. Part of the point was political: the governor wanted a presence north of the bay to block the Russians, who had a co

item.title: 36. The Blue Wing Inn: a gold-rush hotel with a gambling hall
item.description:
Across from the mission is the Blue Wing Inn, one of the first hotels north of San Francisco. It started with the very first property deal in the new town: Vallejo gave the lot to his majordomo, Antonio Ortega, who managed the closing of the mission. The parish priest soon complained about Ortega's treatment of the Native people, and in 1837, after more scandals and doubtful accounts, Vallejo removed him. Ortega stayed on and ran a tavern there until 1848.
In 1849, at the height of the Gold Rush, two men bought it and turned it into a hotel with a gambling hall and a saloon, serving miners he

item.title: 37. General Vallejo: the man in the middle
item.description:
One man appears in almost every story on this side of the hills: Mariano Guadalupe Vallejo. Let's meet him properly.
He was born in Monterey in 1807, the eighth of thirteen children of a Spanish soldier. As a boy he and two other promising youngsters were given private lessons by the governor, with access to his library and newspapers from Mexico City, and an English merchant taught him English, French and Latin. He joined the presidio company as a cadet, and in his twenties was sent north to close the Sonoma mission and command the northern frontier, keeping the Native peoples and the Russia

item.title: 38. The Springs: hot water and Guadalcanal veterans
item.description:
In 1943, ninety veterans of Guadalcanal were sent to a resort here to recover with golf, cherry pie and dances. North of Sonoma, the highway runs through a string of communities known together as the Springs: Boyes Hot Springs, Fetters Hot Springs, Agua Caliente and El Verano. Agua Caliente means hot water. The springs were used and considered sacred by Native people long before the Mexican government granted the land as Rancho Agua Caliente in 1840.
In 1895, a Captain Boyes drilled and struck 112-degree water just 70 feet down, and built a resort hotel. It burned in a wildfire in September 1

item.title: 39. Eldridge: the dark history of the Sonoma Developmental Center
item.description:
Off to the west, near the village of Eldridge, are the grounds of the Sonoma Developmental Center, which for over a century was a large state institution for people with developmental disabilities. It opened here in 1891 as the California Home for the Care and Training of Feeble Minded Children, and Jack London, who lived nearby, set a short story there.
Its history includes one of the darkest chapters of American public health. California passed a compulsory sterilisation law in 1909, the third state to do so. From 1918, the superintendent here, F. O. Butler, was a firm believer in sterilisa

item.title: 40. Jack London and the Valley of the Moon
item.description:
Up on the slopes of Sonoma Mountain, above the village of Glen Ellen, is the ranch of the writer Jack London.
London's life before Sonoma was the stuff of his books. Born in San Francisco in 1876, he was an oyster pirate in the bay as a teenager, sailed to the Klondike gold rush at 21, and came back a committed socialist. In 1903 he sold The Call of the Wild to a magazine for 750 dollars. In 1905 he bought an abandoned winery here and called it Beauty Ranch. He hoped to become a rancher, and between 1909 and 1911 he bought more land to expand it.
Then he began his dream house, Wolf House: 26

item.title: 41. How the Napa Valley was built: volcanoes, faults and gravel
item.description:
Let's talk about the ground under all those vines, because in this valley the geology is the product.
Start with the shape. The Napa Valley is a long, narrow trough between two ranges, the Mayacamas on the west and the Vacas on the east. California's great fault system is about fifty miles wide here, a whole family of faults, including the West Napa Fault, slicing north-west through the region and slowly sliding the land past itself.
Then the volcanoes. In the late Miocene and Pliocene epochs, between about eleven and three million years ago, this area was volcanic. The result is the Sonoma

item.title: 42. Why the Napa Valley isn't covered in houses
item.description:
Notice something about the Napa Valley floor: there are almost no subdivisions or shopping centres between the towns. That's not an accident. It's the result of one of the most important land-use decisions in California history.
Neighbouring Sonoma, Solano and Yolo counties have let large stretches of farmland be rezoned for housing and commerce. In 1968, Napa's vintners and civic leaders went the other way. Using a new state law, the Williamson Act, which gave landowners tax breaks for keeping land in agriculture, they created an agricultural preserve on the valley floor between Napa and Cal

item.title: 43. Volcanic glass of the Valley of the Moon
item.description:
Here's something you can find in the gravel around here: natural volcanic glass. A geology note for this stretch, because the Sonoma Valley is lined with volcanic glass.
The Macrostrat geological maps show, near Glen Ellen and Kenwood, the Glen Ellen Formation: river gravel, sand and silt made mostly of eroded Sonoma Volcanics, and characterised by pebbles of obsidian, natural volcanic glass. Ash layers in it date to roughly 2.5 to 3.3 million years ago. In the hills, the maps show the Rhyolite of Adobe Canyon, glassy grey-to-white lava with contorted, folded flow bands, dated to about 5.3 mi

item.title: 44. Kenwood: the town that couldn't pick a name
item.description:
This next town tried on more names than a teenager tries on outfits. Kenwood sits on what was Rancho Los Guilicos, a Mexican grant of 1837 to a Scottish sea captain, John Wilson, who never lived on it. In 1850 he sold it to another Scot, William Hood, a cabinet-maker who had climbed the mountain above the valley, fallen for the view, and made his fortune building houses in Gold Rush San Francisco to buy it. The peak is now Hood Mountain.
When the railroad came in 1887 and 1888, the little town tried on name after name: Rohrerville, after a land company owner, then Los Guilicos, then South Los

item.title: 45. The Wappo: the brave ones
item.description:
Long before vineyards, the upper Napa Valley was Wappo country. The Wappo homelands spread across the Napa Valley, the south shore of Clear Lake, the Alexander Valley and the Russian River valley. Their language belongs to the Yukian family, distantly related to the Yuki people further north.
They lived by hunting and gathering, in small, independent groups with no central authority, in homes of branches, leaves and mud. Their baskets were woven so tightly they could hold water. Oaks gave acorns, a staple food, and the hot springs at the head of the valley were a place of healing. There were

item.title: 46. Bust: phylloxera, Prohibition and the Depression
item.description:
By 1880, the Napa Valley was booming. There were 443 vineyards with a thousand or more vines each, most of them around St. Helena, and by the end of the century there were more than 140 wineries. Then came three blows in a row.
The first was tiny: phylloxera, a louse that attacks grapevine roots. It killed many of the vines throughout the valley. The answer, which Georges de Latour of Beaulieu helped bring in, was rootstock that resisted the pest.
The second was Prohibition, enacted in 1920. Many wineries simply shut down. A few survived by making sacramental wine for churches, and growers w

item.title: 47. The Judgment of Paris
item.description:
Here's the story that put this valley on the world map.
In the early 1970s, some California wines were outstanding, but hardly anyone noticed; the market wanted French labels. A British wine merchant in Paris, Steven Spurrier, who mainly sold French wine, organised a tasting with his American colleague Patricia Gallagher to mark America's bicentennial. On the 24th of May 1976, eleven judges, most of them French wine experts, tasted top Chardonnays and Cabernets blind, French against Californian, scoring each out of twenty. Spurrier expected the French to win.
They didn't. In both categories,

item.title: 48. Wine country on fire: 2017, 2020, and the insurance crisis
item.description:
Driving through these hills, you'll see blackened trunks and new houses where old ones stood. This is the story of the fires.
On the night of Sunday the 8th of October 2017, hot, dry Diablo winds were gusting up to seventy miles an hour across Northern California. Over a dozen wildfires broke out that night. One started at 9:43 p.m. near Tubbs Lane, in the rural north of Calistoga. Pushed by north-easterly winds, the front of the Tubbs Fire moved more than twelve miles in its first three hours, through the Mark West Springs area and into the city of Santa Rosa. It destroyed more than 5,600 st

item.title: 49. Hot ground: the Sonoma Volcanics, Clear Lake and The Geysers
item.description:
You're crossing the Mayacamas Mountains, and almost everything around you was once molten.
The rock is called the Sonoma Volcanics: obsidian, pumice, tuff, rhyolite, andesite breccia and basalt lava, several thousand feet thick. It forms most of the mountains around the Napa and Sonoma valleys, and it probably once formed a continuous mass from San Pablo Bay north into Lake County, and from Solano County west to the Santa Rosa plain. Geologists think it erupted from several vents, on and off, over perhaps more than a million years, mostly in the Pliocene, three to five million years ago. It's

item.title: 50. The Rodgers Creek Fault: the Hayward Fault's northern half
item.description:
Somewhere beneath this part of Santa Rosa runs one of the most dangerous faults in the Bay Area.
The Hayward Fault, which runs under Berkeley, Oakland and Hayward, has a northern counterpart on this side of the bay: the Rodgers Creek Fault, which passes through Santa Rosa. In 2016, researchers showed the two are linked under San Pablo Bay, forming one Hayward-Rodgers Creek Fault about 120 miles long, from north of Healdsburg to San Jose. Like the San Andreas, it's a right-lateral fault: stand on one side, and the other side slides to your right. It takes up its share of the motion between the

item.title: 51. The Grape King of California
item.description:
Here's a wine story you won't hear in many tasting rooms.
California's first wine grape was the Mission grape, brought by the Spanish, and it dominated California wine until about 1880. The Gold Rush created a thirsty market, and pioneers like Agoston Haraszthy imported cuttings from 165 of Europe's great vineyards. Charles Krug, a Prussian political dissident, learned the trade as Haraszthy's apprentice in Sonoma before founding his own winery in St. Helena.
North of Santa Rosa, at the utopian colony of Fountain Grove, the vineyards were run by Nagasawa Kanaye. He became known as the Grape

item.title: 52. Santa Rosa: the slaughtering place and the Carrillo adobe
item.description:
Santa Rosa has a creek named after a slaughtering place. More on that in a second. You're in Santa Rosa, the largest city in California's wine country and the county seat of Sonoma County.
Before Europeans arrived, the Santa Rosa plain was home to a powerful Pomo group called the Bitakomtara, who controlled the area tightly: outsiders needed permission to pass, and faced harsh penalties if they didn't ask. They gathered for ceremonies on Santa Rosa Creek, near today's Spring Lake. Colonisation brought violence, land seizure, enslavement and smallpox, and the population was devastated, though

item.title: 53. Charles Schulz, Snoopy and the ice rink
item.description:
Santa Rosa was the home of Charles Schulz, creator of Peanuts, Charlie Brown and Snoopy. Schulz grew up in Saint Paul, Minnesota, the son of a barber, and loved ice hockey. He moved to Northern California with his family in 1958, and kept drawing Peanuts until his death in 2000.
In 1969, he and his first wife Joyce built an ice rink here, the Redwood Empire Ice Arena, known to everyone as Snoopy's Home Ice. It has a café called the Warm Puppy, and every summer it hosts Snoopy's Senior World Hockey Tournament, with sixty-odd teams of older players from around the world. Schulz was inducted int

item.title: 54. Luther Burbank: the plant wizard of Santa Rosa
item.description:
Near downtown Santa Rosa is the house and garden of Luther Burbank, one of the most famous plant breeders who ever lived.
He was born in Massachusetts in 1849, the thirteenth of fifteen children. As a young man on a small farm there, he developed a new potato, sold the rights for 150 dollars, and used the money to come to Santa Rosa in 1875. Here, inspired by Charles Darwin's writing on plant and animal breeding, he set up greenhouses and experimental fields and crossed plants on a huge scale. Over 55 years he developed more than 800 strains and varieties: the Shasta daisy, the Santa Rosa plu

item.title: 55. Believe It or Not: Robert Ripley of Santa Rosa
item.description:
Robert Ripley, born in Santa Rosa in 1890, turned weird facts into an empire. He left high school after his father died, worked as a newspaper sports cartoonist from the age of sixteen, and moved to New York in 1913. In December 1918 he drew his first Believe It or Not! cartoon of strange feats and facts. Readers loved it, and sent in their own oddities: unusually shaped vegetables, strangely marked pets.
He took accuracy seriously enough to hire a full-time researcher, a polyglot named Norbert Pearlroth. In 1929 the newspaper magnate William Randolph Hearst syndicated the panel in 360 newspa

item.title: 56. The Coast Miwok
item.description:
The country from the Golden Gate north to the Sonoma coast, and east as far as Sonoma Creek, belonged to the Coast Miwok. That includes the hills around Sebastopol and Freestone and the lower Sonoma Valley.
The Coast Miwok lived in small bands without a central government. In spring they went to the coast for salmon, shellfish and seaweed. The rest of the year, acorns from black and tanoaks were the staple, along with deer and rabbit. Hunters rubbed themselves with a plant called Brewer's angelica to hide their scent from deer. They used yerba buena tea as medicine, burned poison oak to make

item.title: 57. Sebastopol: a bar fight and the Gravenstein apple
item.description:
Welcome to Sebastopol, which has one of the best names on the map. The settlement was originally called Pine Grove. In the late 1850s, so the story goes, a bar fight broke out, and a bystander compared the long-running brawl to the Allied siege of the Russian port of Sevastopol in the Crimean War, which had ended a few years earlier. The name stuck, and Pine Grove survives only in the name of the general store downtown. And remember the Yountville story: that town was first named Sebastopol too, and had to change because this one got there first.
The Coast Miwok and Pomo were here first, and

item.title: 58. Burbank's Gold Ridge farm and the electric railway
item.description:
Luther Burbank needed more room than his Santa Rosa garden allowed, so in 1885 he bought a farm here in what was called the Gold Ridge district, chosen for its variety of slopes, exposures and elevations. At its peak, some estimates put the number of experiments running on the farm at over 60,000, with up to twenty workers. Three acres survive, with over 250 living plants from Burbank's work, looked after entirely by volunteers.
Sebastopol also had an electric railway. From 1903 to 1947, the Petaluma and Santa Rosa Railway ran trolleys and freight around the county, set up partly to break the

item.title: 59. Sebastopol's sea-floor sandstone
item.description:
Here's a surprise for a town twenty miles inland. On the Macrostrat maps, Highway 116 north of Sebastopol runs for more than ten kilometres across the Wilson Grove Formation, a pale, buff-weathering sandstone laid down in the sea between the late Miocene and late Pliocene, roughly eleven to three million years ago. It locally contains beds of shell hash, broken-up mollusc and snail shells, plus pebble conglomerate and volcanic ash. In other words, much of the Gold Ridge country around Sebastopol is an old sea floor, lifted up as the Coast Ranges rose.
To the east, by contrast, the Santa Rosa

item.title: 60. Graton: the edge of the Russian empire
item.description:
Graton, just off the highway, is a little apple town turned wine town, with a big claim: it lies roughly at the furthest south-eastern reach of Russian colonisation in the Americas.
The Russians of Fort Ross, on the coast, needed food. So in 1836 their agronomist, Yegor Chernykh, set up a farm on Purrington Creek, between today's Occidental and Graton, with barracks and five other buildings. He grew vegetables, fruit and wheat, and he also planted a large vineyard, introducing what would become the area's major crop.

item.title: 61. Cannabis: California's other crop
item.description:
Wine isn't the only crop with a complicated legal history in Northern California.
California has been at the forefront of cannabis politics for half a century. In 1972 it held the nation's first ballot initiative to legalise cannabis, Proposition 19, which failed. In 1996, Proposition 215, the Compassionate Use Act, made California the first state to legalise medical cannabis, with 56 percent of the vote. And in November 2016, Proposition 64 legalised recreational use, with 57 percent. Under that law, cities and counties can't stop adults from growing small amounts for their own use.

item.title: 62. Meeting the Russian River
item.description:
Welcome to the Russian River, the last leg of the journey. It's the second-largest river in the Bay Area after the Sacramento, with a main stem 115 miles long, flowing south from Mendocino County and then west to the Pacific.
It has had a lot of names. The Southern Pomo called it Ashokawna, east water place, and also Bidapte, big river. A Spanish land grant of 1843 called it the Rio Grande. Its current name comes from the Russian-American Company, which ran the fur-trading colony at Fort Ross on the coast in the early 1800s. A Russian explorer, Ivan Kuskov, travelled up the river, and an 1817

item.title: 63. California's first commercial sawmill
item.description:
California's first commercial water-powered sawmill was built right around here, and the river destroyed it a few years later. The land around Forestville and Mirabel was once Rancho El Molino, the Ranch of the Mill. It was granted in 1833 to John Bautista Rogers Cooper, a sea captain who'd married General Vallejo's sister. The grant had a strategic purpose: the Mexican authorities wanted settlers pushing west toward the coast to counter the Russian presence at Fort Ross.
In 1834 Cooper built a water-powered sawmill here, driven by Mark West Creek and cutting redwood. It's recognised as the f

item.title: 64. The Pomo: the people of the Russian River
item.description:
The Russian River is Pomo country. The Pomo lands once stretched from the Pacific coast inland to Clear Lake, but the Pomo were never one nation. They lived in small, independent bands, linked by family and marriage, and spoke seven related languages so different that speakers of one couldn't understand another. Linguists think their ancestors may have reached the Clear Lake uplands thousands of years ago, and later spread into the Russian River valley.
The name itself is a happy accident of history. In one Pomo language, it meant something like those who live at red earth hole, the name of a

item.title: 65. The Russians in California
item.description:
Today we've met Russians again and again: a river, a mountain, a farm near Graton. Here's the whole story.
Russian traders pushed east across Siberia and the North Pacific, and in 1799 they founded a colony in Alaska, run by the Russian-American Company. Their business was fur, above all sea otter. From 1803, American ship captains took Alaskan Native hunters south on joint ventures to hunt otters along the California coast; between 1805 and 1812 alone, ten American ships with Aleut hunters gathered over 22,000 pelts.
In 1812 the company built its own base, Fort Ross, on the Sonoma coast, in

item.title: 66. Korbel: Bohemian brothers and California champagne
item.description:
Up ahead is a winery that legally prints the word champagne on its labels, and the French can't stop it. On the riverbank near Rio Nido is Korbel, which has made sparkling wine here since 1882. It was founded by Francis Korbel and his brothers, emigrants from Bohemia, who'd also founded a satirical San Francisco magazine called The Wasp. They used the traditional Champagne method, where the wine is fermented a second time in the very bottle you buy.
Korbel still prints the word champagne on its labels, which might make a Frenchman wince. It's legal because of U.S. rules from the 1930s that tr

item.title: 67. Rio Nido: there is no Canyon Five
item.description:
Rio Nido, the river nest, is a little resort village tucked into a redwood canyon. In 1908 a San Francisco fraternal lodge, the Eagles, bought the land and divided it among members, and the place was first called Eaglenest. During the Second World War its dance hall heaved with sailors on liberty and troops heading for the Pacific, and big bands played there. A small excursion boat once ran down the river to Guerneville's beach.
Two local oddities. The town's unofficial slogan is The Moon Is Always Out In Rio Nido. And its roads are named Canyon One, Two, Three, Four, Six and Seven. There is

item.title: 68. Guerneville: from Stumptown to resort town
item.description:
Welcome to Guerneville. Julia, Adam, driver: congratulations, you've made it. First, the name: it's said Gurn-vill, and locals sell T-shirts reading Don't call it Guerneyville, although people have been saying it that way since the 1800s.
The local Pomo used this spot as a summer camp and called it Ceola, the shady place. The redwoods here grew so thickly that local lore says the valley once had the greatest density of living matter on the planet. Then came the loggers. So many trees were cut in the late 1800s that the town's first English name was Stumptown, and the demand for lumber to rebu

item.title: 69. Armstrong Redwoods: the trees the loggers missed
item.description:
Just north of town is Armstrong Redwoods State Natural Reserve, 805 acres of coast redwoods, including old-growth forest. In the 1870s, Colonel James Armstrong set the grove aside as a natural park. After his death his daughter and another local family campaigned with meetings, rallies and car caravans to save this last remnant of the old forest, and in 1917 Sonoma County bought it for 80,000 dollars.
